Antibiotic Prophylaxis During Invasive Dental Procedures in Patients With Prosthetic Heart Valves　- Cross-Sectional Analysis of Japanese Claims Data
abstract: Patients with prosthetic heart valves (PHVs) are at high risk of infective endocarditis (IE). Although antibiotic prophylaxis (AP) is recommended for invasive dental procedures (IDPs), data on routine procedures and prescribing quality remain limited. This study investigated real-world AP practices across a broad range of IDPs and evaluated prescribing quality in patients with PHVs. We conducted a cross-sectional study using a regional claims database in Kyoto, Japan (2017-2024). Among 52,247 IDPs in 3,664 patients with PHVs, the overall AP prescription rate was 9.2%, with higher rates for tooth extraction (47.3%) and oral and periodontal surgery (32.0%) but markedly lower rates for routine procedures. Penicillins were the most frequently prescribed (45.9%), whereas World Health Organization's AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) "Watch" antibiotics, which should be used selectively because of their higher potential to promote antimicrobial resistance, accounted for 38.1% of oral prescriptions. Dental clinics showed a higher proportion of "Watch" antibiotic use than hospitals (odds ratio 9.0; 95% confidence interval 6.9-12.0; P<0.01). Adherence to guideline-recommended preprocedure timing and single-day duration was low (31.7% and 11.2%, respectively). The IE incidence was 0.44% per person-year. A substantial evidence-practice gap exists in AP use during IDPs in patients with PHVs. Regional efforts promoting antimicrobial stewardship, strengthened medical-dental collaboration, and patient education are needed.

title: MRSA-Triggered Disassembly of an Immune-Recruiting NIR Probe for Bacterial Imaging and Clearance
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections remain a major clinical challenge due to increasing antimicrobial resistance and limited strategies for precise bacterial recognition and clearance. Here, we report an immune-recruiting supramolecular amphiphile, Dman-C11, that undergoes MRSA-triggered structural reorganization for activatable bacterial theranostics. Dman-C11 consists of a hemicyanine near-infrared (NIR) fluorophore, a D-mannosamine immune-recruiting motif, and a hydrophobic C11 chain that promotes bacterial membrane association. The amphiphilic architecture drives spontaneous nanoparticle formation with suppressed fluorescence through aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ). Upon interaction with the MRSA membrane, nanoparticle disassembly redistributes the probe within the lipid bilayer, producing a 20-fold fluorescence turn-on response while simultaneously restoring efficient singlet oxygen generation under 655 nm irradiation. The activated photodynamic process induces ferroptosis-like bacterial death characterized by extensive lipid peroxidation and oxidative membrane damage. Meanwhile, the D-mannosamine motif promotes immune-cell recruitment toward bacterial pathogens, thereby facilitating host-assisted bacterial clearance. In murine wound infection and bacterial keratitis models, Dman-C11 achieves approximately 20-fold reductions in bacterial burden without detectable systemic toxicity. This membrane-triggered supramolecular disassembly strategy establishes a single-molecule theranostic approach that links bacterial recognition, activatable imaging, photodynamic antibacterial activity, and immune-assisted clearance for precise treatment of MRSA infections.

title: Clinical impact of third-generation cephalosporin resistance in hospitalized patients with upper urinary tract infections: a retrospective propensity score-matched study
abstract: Third-generation cephalosporins are commonly used as empirical therapy for hospitalized patients with upper urinary tract infections. However, the increasing prevalence of 3GC-resistant Enterobacterales, mainly driven by extended-spectrum β-lactamase production, has raised concerns regarding inadequate empirical treatment and increased carbapenem use. The independent impact of 3GC resistance on outcomes in non-severe UUTIs remains unclear. We assessed whether 3GC resistance was associated with relapse, clinical failure, or mortality among hospitalized patients with UUTIs initially treated with 3GCs. We conducted a retrospective observational study including adults hospitalized for Enterobacterales UUTIs between January 2022 and December 2024 at a French tertiary hospital. Patients with septic shock or requiring urgent urinary drainage were excluded. Patients with 3GC-R infections were compared with those infected by susceptible strains. All matched patients received empirical 3GC therapy. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using demographic and clinical variables. The primary outcome was relapse within one month after treatment. Secondary outcomes were clinical failure and in-hospital mortality. Among 582 UUTIs, 9.1% involved 3GC-R Enterobacterales; 69.8% resistant isolates were ESBL producers. After propensity score matching, 44 pairs were analyzed. Although empirical therapy was initially inactive in most resistant infections, treatment was adapted within 48-72 hours. One-month relapse rates were identical in both groups (9.1% vs 9.1%; p=1.00). Clinical failure and in-hospital mortality were also similar. In hospitalized patients with non-severe UUTIs, 3GC resistance was not associated with worse clinical outcomes after early therapeutic adaptation. Empirical carbapenem escalation should be guided by severity and individual risk factors rather than resistance risk alone.

title: Metagenomic Features of Oral Microbiome in Tibetan Dental Caries Patients: An Exploratory Study
abstract: This study aimed to preliminarily explore the composition and functional potential of oral bacteria in Tibetan patients with dental caries, and to explore potential associations between the observed functional features and the high-altitude living environment and dietary habits. Saliva samples were collected from nine Tibetan individuals with dental caries. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina high-throughput sequencing platform. The obtained genomes were annotated and analyzed using the non-redundant protein (nr) database, Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) database, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes (CAZy) database, Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), and Virulence Factor Database (VFDB). Across the nine samples, seven dominant phyla and ten dominant genera were identified. At the phylum level, Bacillota (44.06%) and Actinomycetota (26.2%) were predominant. At the genus level, Streptococcus (25.96%) predominated. Functional annotation showed that genes and pathways linked to cell wall/membrane biogenesis (32,623 genes) and carbohydrate metabolism (39,616 genes) accounted for a notable proportion of the total, thereby forming an efficient metabolic cascade encompassing carbohydrate uptake, metabolism, and acid production. Furthermore, multidrug resistance-related annotations represented the largest CARD category (53.05%), whereas immune modulation-related annotations predominated in VFDB annotation (52.48%). This study provides a preliminary description of the community composition and functional annotation features of the oral microbiome in Tibetan patients with dental caries, showing prominent annotations related to carbohydrate metabolism and biofilm-associated functions, as well as resistance- and virulence-related annotations. These exploratory findings may serve as an initial reference for future studies on dental caries in Tibetan communities using larger cohorts and experimental validation.

title: Impact of half-amount fertilization patterns on antibiotic resistance gene dynamics in a soil-root-crop system on a long-term manure-amended farm
abstract: Optimizing manure recycling and mitigating antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dissemination are critical for sustainable agriculture. This field study evaluated nutrient-matched half-dose fertilization regimes (T1: organic-chemical mix; T2: organic alone; T3: chemical alone) against conventional full-dose fertilization (TF) and a no-current-season-fertilizer control (CK) along the soil-root-crop continuum. Topsoil under T2 maintained a total nitrogen concentration (1.29 g·kg), showed a comparatively narrow nitrate concentration range (4.59-7.39 mg·kg), and decreased antibiotic residues by approximately 45% (20.41 μg·kg) relative to TF. Hierarchical partitioning showed that soil pH (27.20%) and available nitrogen-related variables had the largest relative explanatory contributions to bulk-soil ARG variation. The rhizosphere-root compartment showed strong microbiome filtering, with the highest relative explanatory contributions from Chloroflexi (96.60%) and WD2101_soil_group (98.10%), whereas bacterial profiles in washed edible tissue samples were most strongly associated with Pantoea and Sphingomonas (combined contribution 23.40%) among the measured genera. Under TF, higher nutrient and contaminant loading was associated with greater enrichment of key resistance genes (fexA, ISCR1, strA, tetQ) in roots and washed edible tissues (BCF> 1.0, TF> 1.0). Under equal macronutrient inputs, T1 and T2 reduced total bulk-soil ARG abundances by 60%-90% compared with TF (p < 0.05), with no significant difference between them. T1 reduced the proportion of manure applied through partial synthetic substitution, whereas T2 retained organic substrate inputs at the reduced rate. Both regimes showed low root and tissue enrichment indices (BCF≤ 0.03, TF≤ 0.04), indicating markedly lower relative enrichment than TF. These findings support reduced-input fertilization as a promising strategy for mitigating resistome pressure; regulatory compliance and food-safety implications require separate evaluation.

title: Antimicrobial peptides against bacterial pathogens in aquatic and livestock systems: mechanisms, rational design, and translational barriers
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are being investigated for bacterial-pathogen control in aquatic and livestock systems, but their translational evidence is uneven. This narrative review links membrane disruption, intracellular targeting, biofilm inhibition, and host-directed effects to the experimental systems that support each mechanism. Representative piscidins, defensins, cecropins, bacteriocins, and synthetic peptides are compared by assay endpoint and evidence tier. Target-animal infection studies include both protective and unsuccessful interventions, whereas in vitro activity, toxin-injury mitigation, and mammalian-model protection cannot independently establish veterinary efficacy. AMP-antibiotic interactions include synergy, indifference, and context-dependent antagonism, and resistance or cross-resistance can arise. Translation requires route-specific exposure, relevant host-cell safety assessment, and manufacturing feasibility. Biodegradation may limit environmental persistence while shortening effective exposure. AI tools can prioritize candidates, but their predictions require validation in the intended pathogen, animal species, and administration context.

title: Effect of monoterpene-enriched alginate coatings on antibiotic susceptibility of bacteria in brown bear (Ursus arctos) thigh meat during refrigerated storage
abstract: This study investigated changes in the cultivable bacterial community of brown bear (Ursus arctos) thigh meat throughout refrigerated storage and assessed the antimicrobial effects of alginate-based edible coatings containing seven pure monoterpenes: α-pinene, β-pinene, sabinene, D-carvone, bornyl acetate, limonene, and 3-carene. Vacuum-packaged thigh samples obtained from a single brown bear were stored at 4 °C and analyzed on days 0, 3, 5, and 7. Microbiological analyses included enumeration of total coliform count (TCC), total viable count (TVC), lactic acid bacteria (LAB), and Pseudomonas spp. Bacterial identification was performed using MALDI-TOF MS, resulting in the analysis of 1075 isolates representing 34 bacterial species. The composition of the cultivable microbiota changed during storage from an initially high taxonomic diversity (26 species, 8 families), through transient dominance of mesophilic Enterobacteriaceae (70.7% on day 3) and re-detection of Pseudomonas spp. and Moraxellaceae (day 5), to a mixed microbiota on day 7 dominated by Pseudomonas spp. (26.6%), Rahnella aquatilis (11.5%), and Lactobacillaceae (15.5%). β-Pinene, D-carvone, and limonene achieved the greatest reductions in coliform bacteria, ranging from 1.27 to 1.33 log CFU/g compared to untreated controls. In contrast, LAB reached comparable final levels in all monoterpene treatments (5.04-5.15 log CFU/g). Pseudomonas spp. were detected sporadically and generally remained below 3 log CFU/g throughout storage, with no consistent growth pattern observed across treatments. Disk diffusion assays against 34 bacterial species identified α-pinene and β-pinene as the most active monoterpenes (mean inhibition zones of 5.65 mm and 5.29 mm, respectively), while bornyl acetate showed the lowest activity (4.16 mm). Antibiotic susceptibility testing performed according to EUCAST 2025 demonstrated complete susceptibility of all isolates to all tested antibiotics, suggesting a low prevalence of clinically relevant antibiotic resistance phenotypes in the investigated microbiota. This study provides a culture-dependent dataset on bacterial diversity and succession in brown bear thigh meat and shows that monoterpene-enriched alginate coatings moderately reduced the growth of selected bacterial groups while lactic acid bacteria populations were maintained; however, since only microbiological parameters were evaluated, their effect on shelf life requires further verification.

title: Influence of Gliricidia sepium living support on rhizosphere bacterial recruitment and fruit metabolomics in black pepper (Piper nigrum)
abstract: The ability of the rhizosphere to recruit beneficial microorganisms is central to the sustainable management of crops. Here, we investigated, through shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mass spectrometry techniques, the microbial composition, antimicrobial resistance (AMRs), and metabolomic profiles of Piper nigrum cultivated under two support systems: living Gliricidia sepium support (SL/RL) and dead wooden support (SD/RD). Bulk and rhizosphere soils were sequenced to assess taxonomic structure and ARGs, with emphasis on Actinobacteria due to their relevance in antibiotic production. Actinobacteria were highly represented across the samples (~ 35%). Dead-support rhizospheres exhibited a broader ARG repertoire and greater abundance of taxa known to include antibiotic-producing members, whereas living-support rhizospheres showed reduced ARG diversity. Metabolomic analysis further revealed support-dependent physiological responses in the host plant. PLS-DA distinguished the two cultivation systems, and three defense-related flavonoids, such as sakuranetin, isovitexin, and orientin, which were enriched in fruits of plants grown with dead support, indicating activation of stress - and defense - associated metabolic pathways. Their low abundance in living-support plants suggests reduced physiological stress, likely linked to improved nutrient cycling and rhizosphere stability provided by G. sepium. However, the volatile and total phenolic profile did not display significant chemical alterations in the samples. Together, these results suggest that support type influences both microbial functions and plant secondary metabolism. Dead support creates a more stressful ecological context that enriches antimicrobial resistance genes ARGs and defense metabolites, whereas living support promotes a more balanced soil-plant-microbe environment, supporting the use of G. sepium as a sustainable and biologically advantageous cultivation strategy for black pepper.

title: Microplastics amplify Cr(VI)-mediated RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer through coupled interfacial, oxidative, and metabolic regulation
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) can accumulate heavy metals and influence plasmid-mediated antibiotic resistance gene (ARGs) transfer, yet the regulatory mechanisms under metal-associated MP exposure remain poorly understood. Here, a polystyrene microplastic-Cr(VI) composite (PSMPs@Cr) was established to investigate RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer by integrating physicochemical characterization, physiological measurements, transcriptomic analysis, and multivariable modeling. PSMPs@Cr exhibited a non-monotonic effect on conjugative transfer, with the highest conjugative transfer frequency (9.4 × 10) observed at 20 ppm Cr loading, representing a 4.75-fold increase compared with the control. Cr adsorption reconstructed the MP interface by modifying surface charge, wettability, morphology, and colloidal stability, which was accompanied by altered bacterial adhesion behavior. Meanwhile, PSMPs@Cr exposure induced coordinated changes in ROS accumulation, antioxidant responses, ATP production, membrane-associated functions, and energy metabolism. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed treatment-dependent regulation of oxidative stress, membrane transport, cellular communication, and metabolic pathways. Random forest-SHAP analysis identified zeta potential, CAT activity, ATP, and ROS as relatively important variables associated with CTF variation. Overall, PSMPs@Cr-associated ARGs transfer was linked to coupled interfacial, redox, and energetic processes rather than a single regulatory pathway, providing new insights into how microplastic-metal interactions influence plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer under complex contaminant exposure scenarios.

title: Genomic Characterization of Blood-Derived Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae in the Kinki Region of Japan Using Whole-Genome Sequencing
abstract: Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHi)-related invasive disease and antimicrobial resistance are emerging public health concerns, but genomic data on domestic isolates remain limited. We performed a genomic epidemiological analysis of 15 H. influenzae strains isolated from blood samples (n=15) at seven participating medical institutions in the Kinki region of Japan between 2018 and 2020. Whole-genome sequencing with hybrid assembly showed that all isolates were NTHi. Multilocus sequence typing identified 10 sequence types, including recurrent ST165 and ST107, and core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis revealed three clusters, while unclustered strains showed high genetic diversity. Additional pan-genome and Virulence Factor Database (VFDB)-based analyses showed heterogeneous distribution of putative virulence-associated genes, particularly those related to adhesion, iron/heme acquisition, and lipooligosaccharide or outer-membrane structures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that 73.3% of isolates were phenotypically classified as β-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR), while penicillin-binding protein 3 (PBP3) mutation analysis showed that 73.3% were genotypically classified as high-gBLNAR. One ST422 isolate showed reduced susceptibility to moxifloxacin and carried gyrA S84L and parC S84I substitutions. These findings provide regional baseline data on the genomic diversity, resistance mechanisms, and molecular epidemiology of invasive NTHi in the Kinki region of Japan.

title: Prevalence of Genital Mycoplasmas in Pregnant Women and Antimicrobial Susceptibility of Clinical Mycoplasma hominis Isolates in Japan
abstract: Data on antimicrobial resistance in Mycoplasma hominis in Japan are limited. This study investigated the prevalence of genital mycoplasmas, and the antimicrobial susceptibility of M. hominis clinical isolates. Vaginal specimens from asymptomatic pregnant women collected between 2023 and 2024 were analyzed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma parvum, and Ureaplasma urealyticum. Antimicrobial susceptibility of 36 M. hominis clinical isolates collected between 2017 and 2024 was evaluated using the MYCOFAST RevolutioN ATB+ kit, E-test, and LYO2 broth method. Quinolone resistance-determining regions were sequenced in fluoroquinolone-resistant isolates, and tet(M) was assessed by PCR. Among 160 vaginal specimens, the prevalence of M. genitalium, M. hominis, U. parvum, and U. urealyticum was 1.3%, 4.4%, 28%, and 10%, respectively. Resistance rates to levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, tetracycline, and clindamycin were 19%, 11%, 0%, and 2.8%, respectively. Compared with the MYCOFAST RevolutioN ATB+ kit, the LYO2 broth method yielded similar resistance rates for levofloxacin and clindamycin but a higher rate for moxifloxacin. ParC Ser91Ile was detected in all isolates with levofloxacin MICs of ≥4 µg/mL, and GyrA Ser153Leu was additionally detected in isolates with moxifloxacin MICs of >4 µg/mL. Fluoroquinolone- and clindamycin-resistant M. hominis isolates were identified in Japan.

title: Prevalence and farm risk factors for Campylobacter and fluoroquinolone resistant (FQR) Campylobacter from broiler flocks in the United Kingdom
abstract: The increasing occurrence of fluoroquinolone resistant Campylobacter (FQRC) in broiler flocks represents a significant One Health concern. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of FQRC within UK broiler flocks and to investigate farm-level risk factors for Campylobacter and FQRC. Farms from four major broiler companies were recruited into the study. Four boot swab samples were collected pre-thinning on participating farms for microbiological culture targeting Campylobacter and FQRC. Laboratory results were analysed in conjunction with questionnaire data on farm characteristics, management, and antibiotic usage. Multivariable analyses, using a forwards stepwise logistic regression model, was conducted at farm-level. A total of 121 broiler farms were sampled. The prevalence of Campylobacter and FQRC on farms was 28% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 20.0% - 36.0%) and 21% (95% CI: 13.7% - 28.3%), respectively. Rodent presence inside empty buildings (Odds Ratio [OR]=37.2, 95% CI: 3.81 - 363.8), mechanical ventilation with roof chimney extraction (OR= 4.67, 95% CI: 1.24 - 17.6), and beetle spray use (OR= 12.9, 95% CI: 2.47-67.4) were positively associated with Campylobacter. Farms obtaining chicks from fewer hatcheries per crop were significantly less likely to test positive for Campylobacter (1-2 hatcheries per crop OR=0.19, 95% CI: 0.06 - 0.64). Rodent presence inside broiler building anterooms increased the likelihood of FQRC (OR=3.75, 95% CI: 1.07-13.1). Use of mechanical ventilation with a roof chimney (OR=15.60, 95% CI: 3.99-61.3), and rodent presence in empty buildings (OR=23.40, 95% CI: 2.81-195.0) were positively associated with FQRC (which agreed with the Campylobacter model). The study estimated the prevalence of FQRC on UK broiler farms and risk factors significantly associated with increased risk of Campylobacter and FQRC. These findings will provide evidence to guide optimisation of biosecurity for controlling these pathogens in broiler production.

title: Site-Directed Mutagenesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: Precise manipulation of the mycobacterial genome is required to study the effect of specific mutations without confounding influences from the diverse genetic backgrounds in clinical isolates. This is particularly important for interrogating gene function and drug resistance mechanisms, where background mutations may enhance or suppress the effects of a mutation of interest. Here, two targeted site-directed mutagenesis approaches, two-step allelic exchange using a suicide vector and oligonucleotide-mediated recombineering, are described and compared for introducing defined mutations into an isogenic Mycobacterium tuberculosis background. Two-step allelic exchange uses a suicide vector lacking a mycobacterial origin of replication and carrying a mutated DNA fragment, selectable markers such as sacB for sucrose sensitivity, lacZ for blue-white screening, and antibiotic resistance genes (kan or hyg). The process involves generating the mutated fragment via a multi-step polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or synthesis, cloning it into the vector, electroporating it into M. tuberculosis, and selecting single-crossover (SCO) integration events using antibiotic resistance and blue-white colony screening. This is followed by counter-selection with sucrose and X-gal to eliminate bacteria carrying the wild-type sequence. This method ensures stable, unmarked mutations but is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Recombineering uses a recombinase-expressing plasmid, such as pJV75amber expressing Che9c gp61 recombinase under an inducible acetamidase promoter, together with a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) oligonucleotide to introduce precise mutations. Transformants are selected on appropriate antibiotics and confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. This approach is simpler, faster, and more cost-effective, but may be limited by low transformation efficiency, the need for fresh competent cells, and variable efficiency depending on the genomic region and oligonucleotide design. Together, two-step allelic exchange and recombineering offer complementary strategies for introducing defined mutations into M. tuberculosis. Both methods enable experimental validation of mutations, such as variants associated with gene function and drug resistance.

title: Rv0783c of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Acts as a Proton-Motive Force Dependent Multidrug Efflux Transporter Involved in the Efflux of Structurally Unrelated Antibiotics and Enhancing Biofilm Formation
abstract: Despite multiple treatment strategies and extensive research on resistance mechanisms, tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health concern, largely because of the rise of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. Among various mechanisms complicating the situation, active antibiotic export via efflux pumps is particularly significant, yet largely unexplored. Mycobacterium sp. encodes numerous transporters, many of which are overexpressed in clinical isolates or under drug stress. Here, we examined the possible role of Rv0783c, a putative transporter that is reportedly overexpressed in drug-stressed conditions. Rv0783c conferred resistance to multiple structurally diverse antibiotics, fluoroquinolones and anti-TB drugs in the heterologous hosts, namely, Escherichia coli and Mycobacterium smegmatis. Reduced drug accumulation and active efflux of ethidium bromide (EtBr) confirmed its transport activity, which in turn gets nullified upon using the proton-motive force blocker, CCCP (Carbonyl Cyanide m-Chlorophenylhydrazone). On the other hand, its expression enhanced biofilm formation, linking antibiotic resistance to persistence-associated phenotype. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis confirmed the presence of crucial interacting residues with antibiotics that were identified by in silico analysis. Overall, we demonstrate the role of Rv0783c in the extrusion of first and second-line anti-TB drugs and enhancing biofilm formation.

title: Author Correction: Global genomic surveillance uncovers emergence and spatiotemporal patterns of World Health Organization priority antibiotic resistance in invasive Salmonella
Directional spillover of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria from animal, food-production and environmental reservoirs to humans: protocol for a systematic scoping review and causal evidence assessment
abstract: Transmission of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria from animal, food-production and environmental reservoirs to humans underpins One Health policy, yet the causal evidence has not been systematically assessed. Molecular similarity is often invoked as evidence of transmission, but shared resistance determinants cannot establish the direction of transfer. This review will identify and classify evidence on antimicrobial resistance transmission from these reservoirs to humans, generate an evidence map by reservoir category and transmission pathway and identify gaps where policy assumptions outpace empirical support. This systematic scoping review will be reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Global Health and China National Knowledge Infrastructure from 2000 onwards (initial search 16 July 2026; supplementary search 20 September 2026), supplemented by grey literature and citation tracking. Studies linking these reservoirs to human colonisation or infection with antimicrobial-resistant bacteria will be eligible. Records will be screened in duplicate in Rayyan with AI-assisted prioritisation (MetaScreener). Two reviewers will independently assess causal support using a framework integrating evidence type, directionality and level assignment, informed by Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evalution (GRADE) principles and Bradford Hill criteria. Strain-level and gene-level evidence (including metagenomic signals) will be distinguished, and colonisation and infection will be coded as parallel outcomes. The primary output will be a 9×5 evidence map crossing reservoir categories with transmission pathways, showing the highest causal support level, study counts and directionality for each combination. This review analyses existing published data; ethical approval is not required. Findings will be submitted to a peer-reviewed open-access journal, presented at conferences and summarised as briefing materials for One Health policy bodies. The evidence map, extraction dataset and analytic code will be made publicly available through the Open Science Framework (OSF). This protocol is registered on the OSF; registration Digital Object Identifier (DOI): 10.17605/OSF.IO/KQVDC.

title: Antibiotic resistance of bacteria isolated from microbiological control of gastrointestinal endoscopes
abstract: Numerous infections and outbreaks linked to insufficient disinfection of thermosensitive endoscopes have been reported in recent years. The effectiveness of endoscope reprocessing is typically monitored via microbiological controls that detect indicator microorganisms. Resistance profile is rarely assessed in routine surveillance of indicator isolates. To evaluate antibiotic resistance among indicator bacteria isolated from routine surveillance samples of gastrointestinal endoscopes and to determine risk factors for endoscopes' contamination. Antibiograms were performed on all indicator bacteria recovered from control samples of digestive endoscopes at Brest university hospital between 2016 and 2024. A multivariable regression model was done to identify risk factor for contamination. During the study period, 99 distinct indicator bacteria were recovered from 65 endoscope controls. Overall, 15.2% of isolates exhibited acquired antibiotic resistance. Among 41 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, 3 were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins, 6 to carbapenems, and 5 to quinolones. Of 54 Enterobacterales isolates, 17 resisted third-generation cephalosporins (including 6 ESBL producers), 12 were resistant to aminoglycosides, and 12 to quinolones. No carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales were identified. One of three Enterococcus spp. isolates was resistant to amoxicillin. Risk for endoscopes' contamination significantly increased with age of device. This study is the first to evaluate resistance profiles of indicator bacteria isolated from gastrointestinal endoscopes during regular microbiological surveillance. It highlights the potential role of inadequate disinfection in the cross-transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacteria during endoscopic procedures.

title: Epidemiology of multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and performance of molecular genotypic drug susceptibility testing in Papua New Guinea, 2022-2023
abstract: Papua New Guinea (PNG) is a high burden country for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Contemporary data is needed given the introduction of a new MDR-TB treatment regimen. We aimed to describe the epidemiology of MDR-TB from 2022 to 2023 and evaluate the performance of the Xpert MTB/XDR assay in PNG. Molecular testing was conducted at district/provincial laboratories and the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL), and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) at the Queensland Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory. We included cases with Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and MTB/XDR results to describe the epidemiology of MDR-TB. Specimens with Xpert MTB/XDR and phenotypic DST results were used to evaluate the performance of molecular testing modalities compared to phenotypic DST. 206 MDR-TB and 20 pre-XDR-TB diagnostic cases were included, predominantly from Western Province (111, 49%; 18.5 referred cases/100,000 population/year) and National Capital District (86, 38%; 5.7 referred cases/100,000 population/year). The most common risk factor was MDR-TB exposure (67/226, 30%). The Xpert MTB/XDR assay showed high sensitivity and specificity for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance. PNG continues to have a remarkably high incidence of MDR-TB. Risk factor data highlights the importance of contact management. Despite challenges, molecular diagnostics perform well and can improve MDR-TB detection.

title: Dual therapy is associated with synchronous gonococcal susceptible-zone MIC dynamics: Norway, 2013-2025
abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has repeatedly overcome every antibiotic class deployed against it. Antimicrobial resistance surveillance systems that focus on resistance prevalence may contribute to delayed realisation that a bacterial population is adapting to empiric treatment regimes. As new antibiotics zoliflodacin and gepotidacin will soon be launched in Norway, this study aimed to explore how surveillance might detect subtle gonococcal minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) shifts, by focusing on the susceptible-zone, using the dual therapy era as a 'natural experiment'. We also aimed to map the population antibiotic co-resistance landscapes that will confront the new antimicrobial agents. In this retrospective, population-based, descriptive study, the recently introduced 'susceptible isolate pressure indicator' ratio (SIPI) was applied to 13 years of per-isolate Norwegian gonococcal surveillance data (2013-2025; n = 8,230 isolates) to characterise susceptible-zone MIC dynamics during and after the dual therapy era. Annual Kendall τ-b correlations between full MIC distributions of the dual therapy agents and legacy antibiotics were plotted to characterise the evolving cross-resistance landscape. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin SIPI trajectories moved in close synchrony throughout the dual-therapy period and diverged after the 2020 treatment policy change. Divergence timing differed by anatomical site. Male anal and pharyngeal isolates followed distinct trajectories. Post-dual therapy, ceftriaxone and azithromycin SIPI trends were consistent with model predictions for changing selective pressure. Susceptible-zone MIC distributions may contain resistance emergence information not captured by conventional surveillance metrics. The SIPI ratio may offer an innovative framework for monitoring future treatment policy decisions.

title: Occurrence of macrolide antibiotics in drinking water sources and their potential health risks
abstract: Macrolide antibiotics (MLAs) are widely utilized in both human and veterinary medicine. Their extensive use has led to ubiquitous contamination in aquatic environments, posing significant risks to public health and ecosystems. Despite their prevalence, comprehensive analyses of their environmental fate, diverse exposure pathways, and potential molecular toxicological mechanisms remain insufficient. This study systematically reviewed MLAs in global drinking water sources from 2005 to 2025 and their potential impacts on health. Using VOSviewer for bibliometric analysis, key research clusters focusing on ecological risks, antimicrobial resistance development, and health outcomes were identified. MLAs are frequently detected in surface and groundwater, with concentrations exceeding 1000 ng/L in specific regions, primarily influenced by seasonal variations and regional industrial activities. Additionally, we assessed how MLAs through the food chain into human dietary sources such as seafood and dairy products. Clinically, MLAs exposure correlates with a range of adverse health outcomes including cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation), hearing loss, obesity, and developmental defects. Five representative toxicity pathways were reviewed: mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy/apoptosis, hERG potassium channel blockade, altered bile acid homeostasis, nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) inhibition, and oxidative stress. The evidence supporting these pathways varies across individual macrolides, and their relevance to exposure through drinking water remains uncertain. By identifying existing research gaps, this review establishes a robust scientific foundation for risk assessment and calls for enhanced oversight to mitigate the environmental and health risks associated with MLAs.

title: Longitudinal evaluation of a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control bundle in a high AMR prevalence ICU
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a major threat in intensive care units (ICUs). We evaluated changes associated with a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control (IPC) bundle in a high-AMR-prevalence setting. This longitudinal quasi-experimental ICU study (2022-2024) involved sequential, cumulative implementation of a bundle integrating infection prevention, rapid diagnostics and colonization screening, antimicrobial stewardship, and surveillance with data feedback. Hand hygiene compliance increased from 29.5% at baseline to 64.6% during sustainment, while PPE compliance increased from 67.1% to 73.3% after monitoring was introduced. Piperacillin/tazobactam consumption increased (+3.33 DDD/100 patient-days per phase; 95% CI, 1.92-4.73), whereas colistin (-5.85; 95% CI, -9.17 to -2.54) and tigecycline (-2.50; 95% CI, -4.25 to -0.75) decreased. Klebsiella pneumoniae meropenem resistance decreased (OR per phase, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.43-0.69), whereas colistin resistance showed a borderline increase in Acinetobacter baumannii (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.00-1.65). ICU-acquired bloodstream infections decreased across implementation phases for CRE (IRR per phase, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.26-0.51) and CRAB (IRR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.46-0.68), as did CLABSI (IRR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.56-0.73) and ICU-acquired rectal colonization with CRE (IRR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.63-0.84) and CRAB (IRR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.70-0.87), whereas CRPA ICU-acquired colonization increased (IRR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.32-1.85). IPC bundle implementation was followed by improved IPC practices and reductions in several ICU-acquired infections and colonization outcomes; continued surveillance and stewardship are essential.

title: Plasmid-plasmid interactions reshape extracellular vesicle cargo and antimicrobial resistance gene transfer potential
abstract: Plasmids are major drivers of bacterial horizontal gene transfer, including transfer of antimicrobial resistance. Plasmid dissemination extends beyond conjugation to include extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated transport. Although bacterial EVs can carry plasmid DNA, mechanisms governing which plasmids are incorporated into EVs remain poorly understood. Here, we tested whether principles of conjugative plasmid transfer, including effects of plasmid mobility type and plasmid-plasmid interactions, extend to EV-mediated export. Using model conjugative (pKJK5) and mobilizable (RSF1010) resistance plasmids in two independent hosts, we quantified plasmid incorporation into EVs under single- and dual-plasmid conditions. Despite its lower intracellular copy number, the conjugative pKJK5 was preferentially incorporated into EVs, exceeding RSF1010 by 10- to 23-fold under single-plasmid carriage. Under co-residence, this pattern reversed: RSF1010 enrichment increased by 13- to 39-fold, whereas pKJK5 incorporation decreased by 2- to 7-fold, strongly deviating from stochastic expectations based on intracellular abundance, with effects conserved across hosts. This indicates that mobilizable plasmids exploit conjugative transfer machinery to access membrane-associated sites of preferential EV formation, thereby increasing their likelihood of EV incorporation. This demonstrates that EV cargo composition is not stochastic but is actively reshaped by plasmid-specific properties and plasmid-plasmid interactions, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism influencing gene transfer in microbial communities.

title: A dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle delivery system for precision phage therapy against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria
abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among Gram-negative bacteria, demands innovative therapeutic strategies. Here, we present a dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle-chimeric phage (AbLCP) system engineered to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria. Our design integrates a genetically modified M13 phage displaying anti-lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antibodies with polymyxin B conjugation, which is further encapsulated within anti-LPS antibody-functionalized lipid nanoparticles. This system overcomes the fundamental limitations of conventional phage therapy, enabling efficient cellular internalization, endosomal escape, and potent intracellular bactericidal activity. In murine models ofinfection, AbLCP achieved superior bacterial clearance and up to 10-fold reduction in bacterial burden at a 10-fold lower effective dose than free polymyxin B, with 67-fold selective accumulation at infection sites, and attenuated systemic inflammation and preservation of gut microbiota. Mechanistically, AbLCP neutralized LPS to suppress inflammation and induced a lethal bacterial stress response. This work establishes a transformative nanophage platform that merges synthetic biology with nanomedicine, offering a promising strategy against MDR bacterial infections.

title: Molecular Glue Degraders of TEM β-Lactamases by Periplasmic Protease DegP
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the most serious challenges to global health, yet the development of new molecules with novel mechanisms of action to combat resistance is lacking. In this study, we report the discovery of molecular glues that recruit TEM-family β-lactamases to the bacterial protease DegP for degradation. β-Lactamase inhibitor tazobactam was found to accelerate degradation of TEM β-lactamases by DegP, which was further enhanced by linkerless incorporation of dipeptide motifs enriched among DegP substrates. The resulting molecular glue degraders showed improved synergy with β-lactam piperacillin against resistant Escherichia coli compared to tazobactam, as well as good pharmacokinetic properties for oral dosing. Collectively, this work establishes periplasmic targeted protein degradation as a promising new mechanism for combating β-lactamase resistance.

title: Occurrence of carbapenemase genes and phenotypic colistin resistance in wastewater from Kütahya, Türkiye
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global threat that requires coordinated, international action. Recent work highlights how AMR in surface waters affects ecosystems, agriculture, and human health within a One Health framework. The spread of resistance is driven by widespread antibiotic use, self-medication, and inadequate treatment. This study evaluated microbial density and the prevalence of carbapenemase and colistin resistance genes in wastewater treatment plants in Kütahya, Turkey, incorporating seasonal variation. Using conventional and molecular microbiology approaches qualitative and targeted qPCR analysis a total of 60 wastewater samples were screened for key resistance determinants. Multiple carbapenemase genes were detected, including bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, and bla, with blaand blabeing the most frequent. Numerical differences in resistance-gene detection frequencies were observed between the two sampling periods; however, these differences were not statistically significant. bla, bla, and blapredominated in summer, whereas bla, bla, and blawere more common in winter. Mobilized colistin resistance genes (mcr) mcr-1 to mcr-5 were not detected in any of the 60 wastewater samples under the assay conditions used, while the number of detected resistance genes per sample ranged from zero to seven. Overall, the results indicate that wastewater treatment systems may represent important environmental reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance determinants, raising concerns regarding their potential dissemination into receiving environments and underscoring the need for continued surveillance and effective wastewater management.

title: Emergence of vancomycin-resistant and multidrug-resistant Enterococcus spp. in freshwater aquaculture systems of southeastern Nigeria: implications for one health surveillance
abstract: Freshwater aquaculture is increasingly recognised as a reservoir for antimicrobial-resistant bacteria with consequences for human, animal, and ecosystem health. This study characterised Enterococcus spp. from aquaculture systems in Owerri, southeastern Nigeria. Eighty-three specimens were collected from four fishponds: fish body swabs, pond wall swabs, sediment, and surface water. Enterococci were isolated on selective agar and identified phenotypically; a subset of 60 isolates (50% of the collection) was confirmed by 16 S rRNA gene sequencing. Susceptibility to ten agents was tested by Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion following CLSI guidelines, and the sequenced subset was screened by PCR for resistance determinants. A total of 120 isolates were obtained: E. faecalis (37.5%), E. faecium (25.8%), and unresolved Enterococcus spp. (36.7%). Sequencing confirmed 90% of phenotypic identifications and reassigned 10% as E. hirae, E. casseliflavus, or E. faecium. Resistance was highest against vancomycin (75.8%), quinupristin/dalfopristin (71.7%), erythromycin (65.8%), and ciprofloxacin (65.8%). Among the 100 isolates resistant to at least three agents, all had MAR indices above 0.2, and 31 resisted all ten agents. Multivariable analysis linked surface water recovery (OR 3.24; 95% CI 1.42-7.39) and MAR ≥ 0.6 (OR 4.56; 95% CI 1.89-11.02) with vancomycin resistance. Sixty-two resistance patterns indicated substantial diversity. These findings position Nigerian freshwater aquaculture as a reservoir for clinically relevant resistance, supporting antimicrobial stewardship and One Health surveillance.

title: Virulence and genetic determinants of Staphylococcus spp. in human mastitis: a prevalence study
abstract: Lactational mastitis is a common inflammatory breast disease affecting breastfeeding women and is associated with Staphylococcus spp. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and virulence among these pathogens complicate treatment and emphasize the need for accurate laboratory diagnostic methods. This study investigated the microbiological profile, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence characteristics of Staphylococcus spp. isolated from lactational mastitis and evaluated the correlation between phenotypic and molecular detection of major virulence and methicillin-resistance determinants. A cross-sectional study was conducted in central Gujarat, India, using 180 human milk samples collected from 150 women with lactational mastitis and 30 healthy lactating controls. Somatic cell count, bacterial isolation, biochemical identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, haemolysis, slime production, biofilm assays, polymerase chain reaction detection of the hla, icaA, and mecA genes, and phylogenetic analysis were performed. All mastitis samples exhibited somatic cell counts exceeding 1,000 cells/µL, whereas healthy controls remained below this threshold (p < 0.001). Staphylococcus spp. accounted for 89.4% of isolates. The icaA, hla, and mecA genes were detected in 76.39%, 54.65%, and 46.58% of isolates, respectively. Phenotypically, biofilm formation, alpha-haemolysis, and cefoxitin resistance were observed in 72.67%, 52.79%, and 37.88% of isolates, respectively. Excellent agreement was observed between the corresponding phenotypic and molecular findings, with κ values of 0.89 for icaA/biofilm formation, 0.97 for hla/alpha-haemolysis, and 0.89 for mecA/cefoxitin resistance. Elevated somatic cell count effectively distinguished mastitis from healthy controls. The high prevalence of virulent and antimicrobial-resistant Staphylococcus spp., particularly mecA-positive isolates, underscores the need for continuous surveillance, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and cost-effective phenotypic screening to support routine clinical diagnosis and epidemiological monitoring.

title: Putative conjugative transfer and persistence of carbapenem resistance gene bla(OXA-72) from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRA) has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in clinical settings. In this study, we explored the transfer potential of a mobilizable plasmid-harboringgene betweenspecies originating from patients, municipal wastewater, and pig farm wastewater. PCR-based evidence suggested putative transfer offromto. In this pair, the apparent frequency of PCR-marker-positive putative transconjugants varied depending on temperature and meropenem supplementation, with a higher frequency observed at 27°C than at 17°C and 37°C. Likewise, the presence of antibiotic pressure yielded a higher apparent conjugation frequency; however, this observation was limited to a single donor-recipient pair. Further, we revealed a phenotypic conversion in terms of meropenem susceptibility and a fitness cost in the putative transconjugants. While whole-genome sequencing did not conclusively verify the presence ofor a fully resolved plasmid configuration, Oxford Nanopore read mapping consistently detected the chromosomalgene in all isolates. In contrast, only a limited number of reads aligned with thegene,, or the complete plasmid sequences. Comparative analyses further revealed variations in the composition of surface-associated factors and defense systems of the recipient strains, which could be considered as barriers to conjugation. Lastly, the persistence of PCR-detectable marker genes in putative transconjugants was variable and generally unstable over a 30-day period. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into the factors that may influence horizontal gene transfer and short-term maintenance of.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant(CRA) is a serious clinical concern linked to elevated morbidity and mortality. This study shed light on how the carbapenemase genespreads in the environment via horizontal gene transfer. Using isolates ofandfrom municipal wastewater treatment plants, we show that PCR-based evidence of putative conjugative transfer of thegene depends on temperature and antibiotic exposure. The process also incurs fitness costs, and the transferred gene persists only briefly in recipient cells. These results emphasize the importance of environmental sources as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance gene exchange. Additionally, variations in surface structures and defense systems may act as potential barriers to conjugation. Overall, the work improves our understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) movement and supports the need for better integrated surveillance under a One Health approach.

title: Comparative distribution of antimicrobial resistance genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella from chicken and aquaculture production systems, 2010-2025: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: To compare the prevalence and distribution of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella from chicken and aquaculture production systems and assess regional and temporal patterns of resistance genes, six databases were searched for studies published between 2010 and 2025 reporting AMR genes in non-typhoidal Salmonella. Seventy-six studies met the inclusion criteria, including 68 from chicken and eight from aquaculture. Random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled prevalence. Pooled Salmonella prevalence was 21.0% (95% CI 15.3-28.2) in chicken and 44.3% (95% CI 22.6-68.4) in aquaculture, although aquaculture estimates were based on fewer studies. Resistance genes associated with tetracyclines, β-lactams and sulfonamides were frequently detected, particularly tet(A), blaTEM, blaCTX and sul2. Chicken isolates showed substantial regional heterogeneity, with higher prevalence in the Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia regions. Prevalence of selected genes, including tet(A), sul2, aadA and qnrS, increased across sampling periods. Overlapping AMR gene profiles across chicken and aquaculture suggest interconnected resistance reservoirs that may increase opportunities for human exposure through the food chain, highlighting the importance of integrated AMR surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship strategies.

title: Performance of mCIM/eCIM in Enterobacterales strains co-encoding NDM and OXA-48-like carbapenemases from South India
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRE) are an increasing public health concern, particularly as carbapenemase-producing isolates, such as NDM and OXA-48-like producers, become more prevalent. Rapid and accurate identification of carbapenemases is crucial to guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Although recent epidemiologic data show that CRE increasingly harbor multiple carbapenemases, the performance of common phenotypic tests-the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) and EDTA-modified CIM (eCIM)-has not been well defined in these isolates. We examined the performance of mCIM and eCIM among CRE-encoding NDM, OXA-48-like, or both. We included 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encoding CRE isolates from perirectal swabs collected from patients admitted to two intensive care units at a hospital in South India. Isolates included(53.5%),(41.3%), andspecies (5.3%). Overall, 112 isolates (65.1%) encoded NDM alone, 23 (13.4%) encoded OXA-48-like alone, and 37 (21.5%) encoded both NDM and OXA-48-like. mCIM positivity was 98.2% for NDM, 47.8% for OXA-48-like, and 94.6% for NDM+OXA-48-like encoders; among mCIM-positive isolates, eCIM positivity rates were 99.1%, 91%, and 97.1%, respectively. When compared to molecular carbapenemase gene detection, mCIM/eCIM was highly sensitive for classifying isolates encoding NDM as metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers, but significantly misclassified isolates encoding OXA-48-like as having an MBL or lacking a carbapenemase. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA-48-like co-encoding CRE isolates to date, mCIM/eCIM typically reported these as MBL producers. Carbapenemase-encodinginfections are associated with substantial adverse health outcomes, making rapid and accurate carbapenemase detection essential for guiding antibiotic therapy. Althoughcarrying multiple carbapenemases are increasingly reported worldwide, the performance of common phenotypic assays, mCIM and eCIM, remains insufficiently defined for these strains. In this study of 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encodingisolates from hospitalized patients in South India, mCIM/eCIM consistently classified NDM-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase encoders. Additionally, mCIM/eCIM frequently misclassified OXA-48-like-encoding isolates as either metallo-β-lactamase encoders or carbapenemase-negative, highlighting the need to better understand the mechanisms underlying this variable activity. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA co-encodingisolates reported to date, mCIM/eCIM generally reported co-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase producers. Our results suggest that mCIM/eCIM performance may vary geographically due to variable activity, distribution, and combinations of carbapenemases.

title: Whole-genome Mining of a Lead-resistant Bacterial Strain (Bacillus cereus)
abstract: Heavy metals cause neurotoxicity/neuroinflammation in animals, including humans, and heavy metal contamination of soil/water is one of the major factors in neurodegenerative diseases. Soil bacteria that persist in metal-impacted environments often carry genomic determinants for metal detoxification alongside biosynthetic pathways for the production of structurally diverse secondary metabolites. We combined phenotypic identification, whole-genome sequencing and annotation-based genome mining to characterise a soilisolate (designated as VLR6) recovered alongside five additional bacterial isolates (VLR1-VLR5) from the same sample set. Annotation-based mining to identify heavy-metal resistance genes involved in metal transformation, which is essential for understanding metal detoxification mechanisms and their potential implications for neurodegenerative diseases. Isolates were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (Bruker Biotyper). The VLR6 genome (5,411,809 bp, single contig) was annotated with Bakta v1.12.0 (database v6.0) and screened for acquired antimicrobial resistance determinants with the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database Resistance Gene Identifier (CARD-RGI). Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) were predicted using antiSMASH v8.0.4 (default rules; Minimum Information about a Biosynthetic Gene Cluster 3.0 KnownClusterBlast comparisons) and identified through systematic keyword screening of the Bakta functional annotation. VLR4-VLR6 were identified as, VLR1 as, VLR2 as(within thecomplex), while VLR3 yielded no interpretable spectrum. The sequenced isolate (VLR6) genome encoded 5,504 coding sequences, 108 tRNAs, 39 rRNAs and one clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats array (35.3% GC). CARD-RGI identified 14 antibiotic-resistance-associated loci, dominated by glycopeptide-resistance gene cluster components (vanT/vanW/vanY homologues) andclass A/B1 beta-lactamases. antiSMASH identified 12 complete BGC regions, including an NI-siderophore region matching petrobactin (BGC0000942) independently corroborated by annotation keyword screening of the asb/fpu/fat loci, non-ribosomal peptide synthetases-metallophore region matching bacillibactin and an azole-containing RiPP region matching the thiopeptides thiocillin I/micrococcin P1; six regions returned no significant known-cluster match. Annotation-based mining additionally identified a heavy-metal-resistance gene set including a zntA-annotated Pb(II)/Cd(II)/Zn(II)-class P-type ATPase homologue, a complete ars operon (arsRBC) and two czcR-family regulators. The VLR6 genome carries a genomically confirmed set of BGCs, most confidently a petrobactin siderophore cluster corroborated by two independent methods alongside an annotation-supported heavy-metal-resistance gene set. Phenotypic lead-MIC determination and metabolomic or transcriptomic validation are still required before any bioactivity, neuroactive or otherwise, can be attributed to this strain or its predicted metabolites.

title: Antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Group B Streptococcus isolates recovered from pregnant individuals in Greece
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) remains an important pathogen in pregnancy and a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to investigate the antimicrobial susceptibility profile of GBS isolates recovered from pregnant individuals in Greece. A retrospective observational study was conducted, including 89 non-duplicate GBS isolates recovered from vaginal and rectal swab specimens during routine antenatal screening at a maternity clinic in Athens, Greece, between 2021 and 2025. Bacterial identification was performed using the VITEK 2 automated system, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing was conducted by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) according to the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) criteria. High resistance rates were observed for erythromycin and clindamycin, with 58.62% and 54.55% of tested isolates classified as resistant, respectively. Tetracycline showed the highest resistance rate (89.77%), while most isolates remained susceptible to benzylpenicillin (97.75%) and vancomycin (98.86%). Multidrug resistance was detected in 50% of isolates. These findings underscore the need for susceptibility-guided prophylaxis and ongoing surveillance of antimicrobial resistance in Greece.

title: Metal-organic frameworks for antibiotic removal from water and wastewater
abstract: The persistence of antibiotics in aquatic environments has emerged as a critical environmental challenge due to their extensive use, incomplete metabolism, and continuous release from municipal, hospital, and industrial sources. Their accumulation in water and wastewater systems fosters antimicrobial resistance, disrupts ecosystems, and poses severe risks to public health. Conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon and zeolites often fall short in terms of selectivity, regeneration, and adsorption capacity, necessitating innovative alternatives. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with their tunable porosity, high surface areas, adjustable chemical functionalities, and structural diversity, have attracted significant attention as next-generation adsorbents for antibiotic removal. This review provides a comprehensive discussion of the occurrence and impacts of antibiotics in aquatic systems, followed by a critical evaluation of the adsorption performance of pristine MOFs, MOF derivatives, and MOF-based composites. Emphasis is placed on synthetic methodologies, purification/activation strategies, and mechanistic insights underlying antibiotic-MOF interactions. Furthermore, the study highlights the regeneration potential of MOFs for sustainable applications, compares their performance with conventional adsorbents, and identifies the persisting challenges in stability, scalability, and selectivity. Finally, knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined, focusing on defect engineering, hybrid frameworks, and other critical factors governing efficient application in real wastewater treatment to accelerate the translation of laboratory studies into practical deployment. By consolidating advances and challenges, this work positions MOFs as promising candidates for addressing the global threat of antibiotic pollution in water and wastewater.
